questions.q: What does the primary filegroup always contain?
options: The primary data file (.mdf) and the system catalog
Only the transaction log
Only user-defined secondary files
Nothing until you explicitly add a file to it
questions.explain: Every database has exactly one primary filegroup, and it holds the .mdf plus the system catalog metadata SQL Server needs to find everything else.

questions.q: What file extension do secondary data files use, and what do they belong to?
options: .ndf, and they belong to a filegroup (primary or user-defined)
.ldf, and they belong to the transaction log
.mdf, and they belong only to the primary filegroup
.bak, and they belong to a backup device
questions.explain: Secondary data files use the .ndf extension and are added to a filegroup with ALTER DATABASE ... ADD FILE ... TO FILEGROUP.

questions.q: Why does putting files from the same filegroup on separate physical disks help performance?
options: SQL Server spreads a table's pages proportionally across every file in the filegroup, so I/O can hit more than one spindle
It doesn't help; filegroups have no relationship to physical disks
It only helps the transaction log, never data files
It only matters for tempdb, not user databases
questions.explain: A filegroup is a container; SQL Server allocates a table's pages across all files in that filegroup proportionally to free space, enabling genuinely parallel I/O across disks.

questions.q: What is piecemeal restore, and why does filegroup design enable it?
options: Restoring filegroups individually so the database can come online after the primary filegroup restores, before less-critical filegroups finish
Restoring only the transaction log without any data files
A restore method that requires all filegroups to be restored simultaneously
A feature that only works with a single monolithic data file
questions.explain: Piecemeal restore lets you bring a database online after the primary (and any filegroups marked for immediate recovery) restore, while less-critical filegroups restore afterward.

questions.q: Why mark a historical-data filegroup READ_ONLY?
options: Full backups can skip read-only filegroups most of the time, shrinking backup windows on large databases
It's required before you can add a file to a filegroup
It automatically compresses the data
It prevents the filegroup from ever being restored
questions.explain: Rarely-changing historical data marked READ_ONLY doesn't need to be backed up every time, which is a major win for backup windows on large databases with a clear hot/cold data split.
